articles.title: Prohibition of waiting on Manchester Old Road in Middleton from January 2027
articles.excerpt: No waiting will be allowed on part of Manchester Old Road in Middleton from 5 January 2027, affecting local traffic.
articles.content_html:
A prohibition of waiting will be enforced on part of Manchester Old Road in Middleton from 5 January 2027, impacting local traffic flow.

The restriction will be in place from 8am on Tuesday, 5 January until 6pm on Thursday, 7 January 2027.

No waiting will be allowed at any time on the north side of the road, starting 25 metres east of the junction with Chapel Street and extending 33 metres further along.

This decision was made by Rochdale Borough Council to improve traffic management in the area. The council aims to ensure smoother traffic flow and enhance safety for both drivers and pedestrians.

Residents and commuters should be aware of this temporary restriction as it may affect parking and traffic patterns nearby. Further details can be found on the Rochdale Borough Council website.

Rochdale Borough Council announcement: www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2659/manchester-old-road-prohibition-of-waiting-in-middleton-from-5-january-2027

GMP said it was not seeking any further suspects in connection with these alleged offences.

The charges are allegations. No finding of guilt should be inferred, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

articles.title: Man who died in Baguley Crescent flat fire in Middleton named as David Mills, 67
articles.excerpt: David Steven Mills died at the scene of a fire in his first-floor flat on Saturday 7 November. Police say there are no suspicious circumstances.
articles.content_html:
The man who died in a fire at a first-floor flat on Baguley Crescent in Middleton on Saturday afternoon has been named as David Steven Mills, 67.

Mr Mills died at the scene despite the efforts of firefighters and paramedics. Greater Manchester Police said there are believed to be no suspicious circumstances.

Emergency services were called to the block shortly after 2.30pm on Saturday 7 November.

Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service sent three fire engines, from Blackley, Whitefield and Broughton. Firefighters wearing breathing apparatus used two hose reels to put the fire out.

Police and North West Ambulance Service also attended.

A Greater Manchester Police spokesperson said: "Sadly, a man in his 60s passed away at the scene, despite the best efforts from emergency services."

Neighbours described Mr Mills as a kind and helpful man who was well known on the estate.

Margaret Moulding, who lived opposite him, said: "He was a very helpful man. He was very kind and it's very sad."

She added: "He was known as a legend in the community."

Francesca Estasy, who knew him from the estate, said: "When I found out it was Dave, who has been here as long as me, it was really sad."

The cause of the fire has not been released, and police say their investigations are ongoing.

Officers are trying to trace Mr Mills' relatives. Anyone who can help is asked to contact the Police Coroner's Office on 0161 856 8555.

Source: Greater Manchester Police, Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service, and reporting by the Manchester Evening News. Photograph: Greater Manchester Police.

articles.title: Cranmer Education Trust staff gather for professional development event
articles.excerpt: Staff from Cranmer Education Trust, which operates schools in Middleton and Oldham, convened for a professional development event aimed at improving children's lives through inclusive education.
articles.content_html:
Staff from Cranmer Education Trust gathered for a professional development event called Belong 26 at The Blue Coat School and The Loom in Oldham, aimed at enhancing children's educational experiences.

The event brought together teaching and support staff from the trust's ten schools, including St John’s CE Primary School and Rhodes Green CE Primary School in Middleton.

The focus of Belong 26 was on fostering high expectations, strong relationships, and shared expertise to ensure every child has the opportunity to flourish.

The trust's schools cater to more than 7,500 children and young people across Oldham and Rochdale, prioritising excellence and inclusion in education.

During the event, staff participated in practical workshops covering topics such as inclusive teaching, attendance, safeguarding, and communication. These workshops aimed to equip educators with the tools necessary to understand and address the challenges faced by students, helping them overcome barriers to learning and achievement.

Cranmer Education Trust believes that maintaining high expectations for every child is essential for their success. The collaborative efforts of the staff at Belong 26 reflect a commitment to improving educational outcomes for all students.

articles.title: Free job-search, CV and money advice at Middleton Library today
articles.excerpt: Middleton Library is hosting a free work and skills hub on Monday 9 November, with help for job applications, interviews and managing budgets.
articles.content_html:
People looking for work or help improving their job applications can attend a free work and skills session at Middleton Library on Monday 9 November 2026.

Rochdale Borough Council lists the session from 9.30am until 12.30pm at Middleton Library, Long Street, Middleton, M24 6DU. No booking is needed and adults can simply turn up.

The council says the hub offers advice on finding vacancies and training courses, completing CVs and application forms, preparing for interviews, and managing debt or household budgets.

The session is described as taking place every other Monday, although residents should check the council's events listing for the next confirmed date rather than assuming every fortnightly date will go ahead.

For someone returning to employment, the most useful starting point may be a CV or a specific application they want help with. Anyone seeking support can bring details of the vacancy or course they are interested in, although the council does not state that any paperwork is required.

The council's listing confirms the session is free. For enquiries, contact middleton.library@rochdale.gov.uk.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council event listing, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/579/work-and-skills-hub---middleton-library

articles.title: Elsie Blundell MP attends Middleton Remembrance service as parliamentary wreaths laid across constituency
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell attended Middleton's service, with wreaths laid on her behalf in Heywood, Castleton, Norden and at Rochdale Cenotaph.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell attended Middleton's Remembrance Sunday service on Sunday 8 November, while parliamentary wreaths were laid on her behalf across the constituency.

Parliamentary wreaths were laid in her name at the Remembrance Sunday services in Heywood, Castleton and Norden, and at the service at Rochdale Cenotaph.

In a post shared after the services, Ms Blundell said: "Thank you to those who kindly laid special parliamentary wreaths on my behalf at every other Remembrance Sunday service across my constituency - in Heywood, Castleton and Norden - and at the service at Rochdale Cenotaph."

She added: "I am deeply grateful to everyone who led, organised and attended these services, and to all those who came together to remember the service and sacrifice of those who gave everything for our freedom."

Photographs shared with the post show parliamentary wreaths at several memorials, including the Lest We Forget stone for the fallen of Castleton, and a wreath-laying procession.

Source: Elsie Blundell MP, social media post. Photographs: Elsie Blundell MP / supplied.

articles.title: Bikers in red leave Birch Services for 13th Ring of Red ride around the M60
articles.excerpt: Riders were due to set off from the M62 services at 1pm to form a giant poppy around Manchester, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.
articles.content_html:
Bikers in red were due to leave Birch Services on the M62 at 1pm today for the 13th Ring of Red ride, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.

Riders gather at the westbound HGV parking area of the services, which sit between Heywood and Middleton, before heading along the M62 and joining the M60 at junction 18.

They then travel clockwise around the whole of Manchester's ring road. With every rider wearing something red, the procession is meant to look like a giant poppy encircling the city when seen from above.

Riders could gather from 8am, and organisers said the westbound lorry park would be closed to HGVs from Saturday night until 2.30pm today. More than 1,000 motorcyclists were expected.

Jeanette "Netty" Kiely, who organises Ring of Red M60, told the source the ride was a way of saying "we remember, we care, and we will never forget".

Ms Kiely said seeing the bikes come together each year reminded organisers why they do it. She also praised the Bridge Supporters who stand on motorway bridges in all weathers to wave and cheer as the riders pass underneath.

She added that after 13 years the event had become a community coming together to remember, rather than simply a motorcycle ride.

The Ride of Respect is free to join and non-competitive. It honours members of the Armed Forces past and present and those who died in service.

Money is raised through sales of official red T-shirts, hoodies and patches, with a separate clothing range for Bridge Supporters. Heywood Veterans Association, this year's nominated charity, supports veterans in Heywood, Middleton and surrounding areas.

The Manchester ride grew out of the original Ring of Red on the M25. Ms Kiely has previously said she agreed to stage a northern version after a phone call from the London organiser.

The M60 event's biggest turnout came in 2022, when 5,986 bikes took part, up from 4,400 the year before. Ms Kiely said at the time: "It was incredible to have our highest turn out yet – with 5986 bikes."

Around 3,000 bikers took part last year, according to the Oldham Times. Previous nominated charities include Veterans into Logistics and Veterans in Communities.

Riders finish back at Birch Services once the lap of the M60 is complete.

Source: Ring of Red M60 organisers via the source. Photograph: supplied.

articles.title: Middleton's Veterans' Walk: the poppy mural honouring the town's service men and women on Remembrance Sunday
articles.excerpt: A wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the Middleton in Bloom mural of poppies, a Spitfire and the white cliffs of Dover.
articles.content_html:
A poppy wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the town centre mural that Middleton in Bloom created as a tribute to the town's service men and women, on Remembrance Sunday.

The mural runs the length of a wall in Middleton town centre. A Spitfire trails a stream of red poppies across a painted sky, above silhouettes of soldiers standing among giant poppies, a soldier with a horse, the white cliffs of Dover and a warship at sea.

Planters along the foot of the wall are wrapped in a poppy-print banner carrying the words of Laurence Binyon's poem For the Fallen: "They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old."

The wreath sits beneath the Veterans' Walk plaque, in the planter in front of the painted sea.

The plaque records that the installation was officially opened on 8 May 2025, the 80th anniversary of VE Day, by Ted Woolley OStJ, branch chairman of the Middleton branch of the Royal British Legion.

Middleton in Bloom finished the white cliffs of Dover section in time for VE Day last year, the Rochdale Times reported at the time. The wooden panel had to be replaced, so the sea was painted first and the Spitfire and poppies were added afterwards.

Elsewhere in Middleton, a "Lest We Forget" display of two kneeling soldiers either side of a cross has been planted with red cyclamen and poppies.

Middleton's Remembrance Sunday parade assembled at 10.10am on Long Street this morning and marched to Middleton Memorial Gardens on Middleton Old Road for a service at 10.45am.

More about the group's work is published at middletoninbloom.co.uk.

articles.title: Is there really a secret tunnel under Middleton between the Ring O’Bells and St Leonard’s?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells to St Leonard’s, but formal records and heritage surveys offer no published proof.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells to St Leonard’s, but formal records and heritage surveys offer no published proof.
articles.body:
Short answer: no published, verifiable evidence has been found that a continuous built tunnel links the Ring O’Bells (St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

The story is older and more persistent than the proof. For generations Middleton guides, ghost‑tour pages and regional folklore compilations have repeated a neat Civil War image: Royalists meet in the pub cellar, a hidden passage runs under the road to the church and the plotters slip away when the Roundheads arrive. The tale is still used on commercial ghost walks and local history roundups. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

Where the legend runs into trouble is the documentary and professional heritage record. St Leonard’s is a Grade I listed medieval church whose National Heritage List entry sets out its fabric, phases and sensitivity in detail; that entry makes no mention of a connecting passage. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332)) The Middleton Town Centre conservation‑area appraisal kept by Rochdale Council, the document that describes known historic assets and archaeological sensitivity across the square, likewise does not record any mapped or scheduled tunnel between the buildings. ([planning.data.gov.uk](https://www.planning.data.gov.uk/entity/6313525))

Stories of bones, buckles, muskets and a landlord frightened by a flying stone appear repeatedly in popular accounts and in later retellings of a local newspaper item often cited as the Oldham Evening Chronicle, 18 August 1972. Those secondary sources show how the tale has been told and retold, but I could not find a publicly accessible archaeological report, museum accession entry or digitised press copy that records the 1972 item or the claimed finds to the standard used by heritage professionals. In short: there are repeated claims of finds in folklore and tourism material, and an absence of a published excavation report or archive catalogue entry to corroborate them. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

That absence matters. If a brick‑lined or purpose‑built passage had been known, recorded or opened in modern times it would normally appear in at least one of these places: the national listing or schedule, the local conservation appraisal, an archaeological trust report, or a museum accession catalogue for recovered artefacts. None of those formal records I checked lists a continuous tunnel between the pub and the church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

Does that mean there was no subterranean connection at any point in any century? Not necessarily. Old cellars, drains, short escape routes and rubble‑filled voids are common in historic town centres; people over the centuries may have used cellars and alleys in ways oral tradition remembers as a “tunnel”. The distinction between an occasional informal route (a bricked‑up opening, a man‑hole, a drainage culvert) and an intentionally constructed, continuous tunnel is crucial and is where legend and archaeological standards part company. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

If a reader wants to move the story from local memory to proof, the practical steps are straightforward. Search original local‑paper runs (Rochdale Local Studies and the borough archives hold many microfilm runs and can advise on the Oldham Evening Chronicle reference); ask the Local Studies Centre (Sparth / Touchstones) and Middleton Library about any accessioned finds or records from Ring O’Bells cellars; and, if someone locates artefactual material, have it recorded by an accredited archaeologist and offered to a museum or deposited with the borough collection. The local archives are the place to start for newspaper, court and parish records. ([yourtrustrochdale.co.uk](https://www.yourtrustrochdale.co.uk/venues/local-studies-centre/))

For most Middleton people the tunnel story is less a missing map than a useful piece of place‑making: it links real places (a medieval church, an old inn) to real turmoil (the Civil War) and to the town’s habit of telling itself stories about its past. That is worth recording; just not the same thing as saying the tunnel, as described in the tales, has been demonstrated by archaeology or primary documents. Treat the passage as a well‑rooted local tradition with plausible historical context, and—until someone produces an excavation report or archive copy to the contrary—also treat the physical tunnel as unproven. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))
articles.content_html:
Short answer: no published, verifiable evidence has been found that a continuous built tunnel links the Ring O’Bells (St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

The story is older and more persistent than the proof.

For generations Middleton guides, ghost‑tour pages and regional folklore compilations have repeated a neat Civil War image: Royalists meet in the pub cellar, a hidden passage runs under the road to the church and the plotters slip away when the Roundheads arrive.

The tale is still used on commercial ghost walks and local history roundups. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

Where the legend runs into trouble is the documentary and professional heritage record. St Leonard’s is a Grade I listed medieval church whose National Heritage List entry sets out its fabric, phases and sensitivity in detail; that entry makes no mention of a connecting passage.

([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332)) The Middleton Town Centre conservation‑area appraisal kept by Rochdale Council, the document that describes known historic assets and archaeological sensitivity across the square, likewise does not record any mapped or scheduled tunnel between the buildings. ([planning.data.gov.uk](https://www.planning.data.gov.uk/entity/6313525))

Stories of bones, buckles, muskets and a landlord frightened by a flying stone appear repeatedly in popular accounts and in later retellings of a local newspaper item often cited as the Oldham Evening Chronicle, 18 August 1972.

Those secondary sources show how the tale has been told and retold, but I could not find a publicly accessible archaeological report, museum accession entry or digitised press copy that records the 1972 item or the claimed finds to the standard used by heritage professionals.

In short: there are repeated claims of finds in folklore and tourism material, and an absence of a published excavation report or archive catalogue entry to corroborate them. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

That absence matters.

If a brick‑lined or purpose‑built passage had been known, recorded or opened in modern times it would normally appear in at least one of these places: the national listing or schedule, the local conservation appraisal, an archaeological trust report, or a museum accession catalogue for recovered artefacts.

None of those formal records I checked lists a continuous tunnel between the pub and the church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

Does that mean there was no subterranean connection at any point in any century? Not necessarily.

Old cellars, drains, short escape routes and rubble‑filled voids are common in historic town centres; people over the centuries may have used cellars and alleys in ways oral tradition remembers as a “tunnel”.

The distinction between an occasional informal route (a bricked‑up opening, a man‑hole, a drainage culvert) and an intentionally constructed, continuous tunnel is crucial and is where legend and archaeological standards part company. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

If a reader wants to move the story from local memory to proof, the practical steps are straightforward.

Search original local‑paper runs (Rochdale Local Studies and the borough archives hold many microfilm runs and can advise on the Oldham Evening Chronicle reference); ask the Local Studies Centre (Sparth / Touchstones) and Middleton Library about any accessioned finds or records from Ring O’Bells cellars; and, if someone locates artefactual material, have it recorded by an accredited archaeologist and offered to a museum or deposited with the borough collection.

The local archives are the place to start for newspaper, court and parish records. ([yourtrustrochdale.co.uk](https://www.yourtrustrochdale.co.uk/venues/local-studies-centre/))

For most Middleton people the tunnel story is less a missing map than a useful piece of place‑making: it links real places (a medieval church, an old inn) to real turmoil (the Civil War) and to the town’s habit of telling itself stories about its past.

That is worth recording; just not the same thing as saying the tunnel, as described in the tales, has been demonstrated by archaeology or primary documents.

Treat the passage as a well‑rooted local tradition with plausible historical context, and—until someone produces an excavation report or archive copy to the contrary—also treat the physical tunnel as unproven. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

articles.title: Middleton pupils form giant star to celebrate Rhodes Green school's new name
articles.excerpt: The former Little Heaton primary school welcomed the Bishop of Middleton for a celebration of its new name, with classroom visits, worship and a tree planting.
articles.content_html:
Pupils at a Middleton primary school formed a giant star in their playground to celebrate its new name during a visit from the Bishop of Middleton.

Rhodes Green Church of England Primary School, on Boardman Lane in Rhodes, welcomed the Rt Revd Mark Davies on Thursday 5 November. Children, staff, parents and members of the community joined the celebrations, which included classroom visits, worship and the planting of a commemorative tree.

The school was previously known as Little Heaton CE Primary School. It changed its name in September to reflect its connection with the Rhodes community, where many of its pupils live. Rochdale Council's school directory also records the change.

The star reflected the school's Christian vision, “Shine as stars in the world”, with children lining up in the playground to form its outline for a photograph taken from above.

Headteacher Chloe Noon said: “Rhodes Green is about much more than a new name. It's about the school we're building together and making sure every child feels happy, safe and proud to belong here.”

She added: “We want our children to have big dreams, to believe in themselves and to know that they can achieve wonderful things. Seeing them come together today, and hearing Bishop Mark share that same message, has been really special for all of us.”

The head boy and head girl showed the Bishop around the school, taking him into classrooms to meet children from every year group before an assembly with families. Pupils and staff gave readings during the celebration.

Bishop Mark, who has known the school for more than 20 years, said: “Today has been absolutely amazing and such a tremendous joy and a great blessing. Today represents a new and exciting chapter. A name says so much and is so, so important.”

During a conversation with pupil leaders, he spoke about teachers and church leaders who had encouraged him and urged the children to believe in their own ambitions.

Cranmer Education Trust, which supplied the account of the visit, said the school joined the trust in 2024. Its chief executive Julie Hollis and chair of trustees Janet Gregory attended, alongside the Rev'd Jenni Beaumont from All Saints, Rhodes.

For families who know the school by its former name, Rhodes Green is the same Boardman Lane school. Its current information is available at https://www.rhodesgreen-primary.org/.

articles.title: Who is the 'Sad Cavalier' said to haunt Middleton's Ring O'Bells?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to St Leonard’s, but the formal record does not confirm a continuous, built tunnel.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to St Leonard’s, but the formal record does not confirm a continuous, built tunnel.
articles.body:
If you ask pub regulars and local guidebooks who the Ring O'Bells' ghost is, they'll give you a tidy answer: the Sad Cavalier, nicknamed Edward, a Royalist in plumed hat and cloak who haunts the old inn and its cellars. That account — a betrayed cavalier fleeing through a secret tunnel, murdered at a church exit, and buried under the pub's flagstones — is the version most often repeated in tourism and folklore write-ups, and it is the story behind ghost-hunt events now advertised for the building on St Leonard's Square. (Visit Rochdale’s local history/what’s-on page summarises the tradition in full.)

But legend and archive are not the same thing. What survives in contemporary and older printed sources is two separate threads: first, Middleton's documented seventeenth‑century politics and local gentry; second, a body of later folklore, local recollections and modern tourism copy that stitches a named cavalier to the Ring O'Bells. The reliable historical picture is straightforward: Middleton and its leading families were active in the Civil Wars and, as local histories explain, many local men and some gentry supported Parliament. Nineteenth‑century accounts of the town (for example, Edwin Waugh’s Lancashire Sketches) record Ralph Assheton and others raising men for the parliamentary cause and the wider county’s contested loyalties in the 1640s. Those sources show the town was very much a theatre of seventeenth‑century political division — which makes it an easy setting for a Royalist-versus-Roundhead ghost story.

The Stannycliffe name that appears in the Ring O'Bells tale also exists in the documentary record. County and diocesan antiquarian material mention a house or hall near Middleton called Stannycliffe (older printed collections record people “of Stannycliffe Hall” and deaths there). Those references confirm Stannycliffe as a historic local place‑name and social unit, not a modern invention of ghost tours. They do not, however, identify an “Edward” who was killed at the pub or provide a contemporary 1640s account of the gruesome ambush the legend describes.

What the tradition adds — and what we cannot yet verify from primary records — are the grisly details: a secret tunnel linking the Ring O'Bells' cellar to St Leonard’s church; the discovery of Civil War‑period pikes, buckles or helmets beneath the cellar flagstones; several skeletons dug up and identified as seventeenth century; and a 1972 newspaper report of violent cellar phenomena. These claims are regularly echoed in guidebooks and paranormal sites and are summarised on Visit Rochdale’s event listing, but I could not locate a contemporary archaeological report, museum accession record or an accessible copy of the cited 1972 Oldham Evening Chronicle item while researching this piece. In short: the colourful physical evidence cited in the story appears in modern folklore sources, but I found no published excavation report or council record confirming human remains or a formal 17th‑century burial under the pub.

That distinction matters for readers: Middleton’s seventeenth‑century division and the existence of Stannycliffe give the story a historically plausible frame, but plausibility is not proof. If you want to pursue the matter further, the borough’s Local Studies and Archives holds parish registers, newspapers, maps and estate papers that are the right places to look for contemporary mentions (the Rochdale Local Studies Centre and Middleton library collections are the starting points listed by the council). A verified archaeological report or an indexed newspaper copy would settle whether the cellar finds and the 1972 incidents are documentary facts or later accretions to the tale.

So who is the Sad Cavalier? In Middleton today he is, quite plainly, a figure of folk memory: a Royalist gentleman named in local story, given the friendly if mournful nickname Edward by landlords and guide‑writers. The deeper, verifiable facts are less dramatic — a documented history of local Parliamentary activity in the 1640s and the historic place‑name Stannycliffe — and no clear primary record tying a named Royalist corpse to the Ring O'Bells' cellar has been located in the sources checked for this piece. The legend will keep drawing in curiosity; for readers who prefer evidence to atmosphere, the archives at Touchstones/Rochdale Local Studies and the parish papers are where the next, verifiable chapter would appear.

Sources consulted: Visit Rochdale’s Ring O'Bells entry and event listing for the pub’s folklore; nineteenth‑century local histories recording Middleton’s Civil War activity; and diocesan/antiquarian material that attests to a historic Stannycliffe near Middleton. Where modern guides repeat finds of helmets, pikes and skeletons beneath the cellar I have flagged those claims as unverified pending archival or archaeological confirmation.

articles.title: Middleton residents warned about scammers posing as council officials
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has issued a warning to residents in Middleton about scammers posing as council officials to gain entry into homes.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Middleton are being warned about scammers posing as council officials in an attempt to gain entry into their homes. This warning follows reports of several incidents in the area, prompting Rochdale Council to take action.

The council stated, "We have been made aware of bogus cold callers posing as council officers to gain entry into homes." They emphasised that all legitimate council staff carry identification and can produce it upon request.

Residents are advised to check for ID before allowing anyone into their homes.

If residents are unsure about a caller's identity or if they cannot produce an official badge, they are encouraged to refuse entry.

The council also reminded residents that services and appointments can only be booked and paid for in advance through their contact centre at 01706 647474.

Residents who have experienced similar visits are urged to report them to Greater Manchester Police, either online or by calling 101.

articles.title: Rochdale Council purchases Warwick Mill for £3.3 million
articles.excerpt: The purchase of Warwick Mill and London House marks a significant step in Middleton's regeneration efforts, with plans for redevelopment underway.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's regeneration has taken a significant step forward with the Rochdale Borough Council completing the purchase of Warwick Mill from developer Kam Lei Fong.

The historic cotton mill, built in 1907, has been vacant for over a decade and has become a target for vandalism and urban explorers.

As part of the £3.3 million deal, the council also acquired the neighbouring London House, a 1960s office block that is set to be demolished.

The redevelopment of Warwick Mill is seen as a vital opportunity to restore an important historic building and create new homes for the local community.

Immediate actions include enhancing security at the site with a 24-hour presence from Rochdale firm Winterburns, which will also begin clearing debris, including over 1,000 tyres and overgrown vegetation.

The internal strip-out of both Warwick Mill and London House is expected to commence shortly, with demolition of London House planned for early next year.

Councillor Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed optimism about the redevelopment, stating it will not only improve the area but also provide much-needed housing.

The council will soon begin the process of selecting a developer partner to undertake the long-term redevelopment of Warwick Mill.

articles.title: Boyes opens new store in Middleton Shopping Centre tomorrow
articles.excerpt: Discount chain Boyes will open its new store in Middleton Shopping Centre, filling the gap left by Wilko's closure.
articles.content_html:
Discount chain Boyes is set to open its new store in Middleton Shopping Centre tomorrow, 6 November, at 9am. This new store will occupy the former Wilko site, which closed earlier this year, leaving a gap in the local retail landscape.

For the past few weeks, contractors and staff have been preparing the two-floor space to welcome customers. Boyes aims to provide a wide range of products, including everyday essentials, electrical items, DIY supplies, fashion, footwear, craft and hobby materials, homewares, and seasonal goods.

Local residents have expressed enthusiasm about the new store. Yvonne Marie Knott stated, "Boyes has everything you need in a store," while Sharon Dyson added, "Can’t wait, Middleton needs this."

Kathleen Hall also shared her excitement, saying, "Looking forward to it!"

The opening of Boyes is expected to bring a boost to the local economy and provide residents with a convenient shopping option. As the store prepares to welcome its first customers, it will help fill the retail void left by Wilko's closure.

articles.excerpt: A three-year-old boy is in critical condition following a medical emergency at Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton, with police confirming the incident is not suspicious.
articles.content_html:
A three-year-old boy is currently in critical condition in hospital following a medical emergency at Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton. Emergency services were called to the nursery on Mainway East on Monday afternoon, 2 November, after reports of the incident.

The response involved three police vehicles, an ambulance, and a rapid response paramedic car, with an air ambulance also landing nearby. A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police confirmed that the incident is not being treated as suspicious and that inquiries are ongoing.

Cosy Toes nursery, which is part of a chain operating four nurseries across Middleton, provides daycare for children up to five years old. The nursery has been approached for further information regarding the incident, but no additional details have been released.

As the boy continues to fight for his life in hospital, the community is left concerned about his wellbeing and the circumstances surrounding the emergency. Updates from authorities will be crucial for those affected and the wider community.

articles.title: Middleton care worker celebrated after 27 years at Langfield Care Home
articles.excerpt: Karen Haycock, who joined Langfield Care Home in Langley in May 1999, was surprised by colleagues and residents marking what the home calls 10,000 days of service.
articles.content_html:
A support worker at a Middleton care home has been celebrated by colleagues and residents after more than 27 years of looking after people at the home.

Karen Haycock, a specialist support worker at Langfield Care Home on Wood Street, Langley, was surprised with gifts, flowers and cards at a gathering on 27 October.

The home is marking the occasion as 10,000 days of service. Karen joined the home’s operator, Orchard Healthcare Group, in May 1999 — roughly 10,000 days ago — so the milestone reflects the length of her time with the home rather than a count of individual shifts.

Over her career Karen has worked across residential care, dementia care and nursing. She now works in the home’s Reconnect dementia community, which supports residents living with advanced dementia.

Along the way she completed an NVQ Level 2, took part in Orchard’s Step Up programme and undertook specialist Dementia Promise training. The group says she has seen the sector change considerably in that time, with better specialist training, equipment and more individual approaches to caring for people with dementia.

For Karen, though, the job is still about people. “I love spending time with the residents. They become your family,” she said.

Asked what she would tell anyone thinking about a career in care, she said: “You need to give it 100% to be able to make a difference to people, and that’s the best part.”

Home manager Lisa-Marie Hutchinson said: “Karen’s 10,000 working days is a fantastic achievement, and we were delighted to celebrate this special milestone with her and show her how much she is appreciated.”

Long service of this kind is increasingly rare in adult social care, where staff turnover is high and many homes rely on a changing workforce. For residents living with dementia, a familiar face who has known the home for decades can make a real difference to day-to-day life and to families choosing care for a relative.

Langfield is one of 23 care homes run by Harrogate-based Orchard Healthcare Group across the North of England and the Midlands. The group says the home holds a Good rating from the Care Quality Commission.

articles.title: Rochdale Council approves new Storage World building in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for a new Storage World building in Middleton, following a fire that destroyed the previous structure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has approved the rebuilding of Storage World in Middleton town centre. The planning application submitted by Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd (SSPMI) was greenlit to replace the building on Old Hall Street, which was destroyed by fire in June last year.

The new development will be a £12 million mixed-use building, smaller in footprint but taller than the previous structure.

It will feature self-storage units on the upper floors and commercial units on the ground floor, occupying half the space of the former Storage World but with two additional storeys to maintain capacity.

In their application, P4 Planning highlighted the aim to create a modern design that would not only restore self-storage services but also stimulate small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) activity in the area.

They noted that the design would reflect the historical context of the site, which previously housed Albany Mill until 1975.

articles.title: Middleton schools face financial challenges due to declining pupil numbers
articles.excerpt: Middleton schools are grappling with financial pressures as a significant drop in birth rates is expected to impact primary school enrolments in 2027.
articles.content_html:
Middleton schools are facing financial challenges as a report reveals a significant decline in birth rates, which is expected to affect primary school enrolments in 2027.

The report, presented to township committees, highlights that the borough is experiencing the lowest birth rate for 23 years, leading to concerns about the long-term financial sustainability of some primary schools.

In September 2026, there was a peak in Reception year pupils, but the projected intake for 2027 is only 2,647, the lowest since 2003.

This decline is anticipated to create additional financial pressures for schools that have already seen a reduction in student numbers and an increase in empty seats over recent years.

The report indicates that while there has been an average of 113 children needing places after moving into the borough each year, this figure has dropped to just 20 over the past two years.

An average of 30 pupils per year have not taken up secondary school places within the borough, exacerbating the situation.

As a response to the declining numbers, Rochdale Council has already removed 90 surplus Reception places for September 2024 and an additional 35 for September 2025.

Further reductions are expected in areas where there are too many empty places, highlighting the need for strategic planning to address these challenges.

articles.title: Middleton designated as mayoral development area to boost regeneration
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig has designated Middleton as a mayoral development area, aiming to enhance economic development and housing in the town.
articles.content_html:
Middleton has been officially designated as a mayoral development area by Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, marking a significant step forward in the town's regeneration efforts.

This decision follows a six-week public consultation and was approved by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) last month, with Rochdale Council also endorsing the proposal.

The establishment of the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation is expected to accelerate economic development and regeneration in the area. The GMCA highlighted that this designation presents a substantial opportunity to improve Middleton town centre and its surrounding communities.

The new development corporation aims to attract both public and private investment, facilitating the construction of approximately 1,500 new homes, including affordable housing. This initiative is part of a broader strategy to enhance the living conditions and economic prospects for local residents.

The Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government has been notified of this designation, which will be formalised by an official order.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town’s regeneration journey takes another step forward - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Town’s regeneration journey takes another step forward Regeneration of Middleton has moved a step closer after the town was identified as a mayoral development area by Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig. Following a six-week public consultation, a report was submitted to a meeting of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) last month when the proposed designation was approved and subsequently endorsed by Rochdale Council. The Mayor notified the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government of the designation. The Secretary of State will, by Order, establish a Mayoral development corporation for the Area. The name to be given to the Mayoral development corporation is the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation. Designating the town as a mayoral development corporation is expected to help speed up furthering economic development and regeneration in Middleton. The GMCA said: “The area presents a significant opportunity to improve Middleton town centre and its surrounding communities. “Establishing the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation will help attract public and private investment, bring forward new development and support the delivery of around 1,500 new homes, including affordable homes. READ MORE: New trial gives children better mental health and social care support Middleton has been identified as a mayoral development area. Image: GMCA “It will also strengthen the town’s commercial and leisure offer, improve public spaces and infrastructure, create jobs and support better services for local people. “Without a dedicated delivery vehicle, Middleton would risk missing the opportunity to coordinate investment, accelerate regeneration and overcome barriers relating to land, infrastructure, viability, funding and delivery.” The corporation will be underpinned by co-operative principles, giving residents, businesses and community organisations a meaningful voice in shaping the regeneration programme. This approach will help ensure that investment delivers inclusive growth, social wellbeing, community pride and benefits that extend across Middleton and the wider borough. The corporation is expected to be established in early 2027. It will provide a single, focused body for local decision-making and engagement with residents, communities, government departments, public agencies, landowners, developers and investors. Working alongside Rochdale Council, Rochdale Development Agency and GMCA, it will coordinate delivery and help secure public and private investment to realise the shared vision for regeneration across the Area. articles.excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
articles.content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts.

A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts.

Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies.

As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. Adrian Abraham, from Middleton, only started playing the guitar about two years ago. Later this month, he is taking the Trinity College London Grade 8 Rock & Pop electric guitar examination — and could win a Guinness World Record in the process. Adrian loves heavy metal and picked up the guitar after hearing his father, Abraham Joseph, play the acoustic guitar. His favourite band is Iron Maiden and his favourite song to play is Eruption, by Van Halen. His Instagram page features dozens of videos chronicling his journey, including performances of hits by Metallica, Guns ‘n’ Roses, Queen, Deep Purple, Slipknot and System of a Down. The youngster said: “I saw my dad playing the guitar and I thought it really sounded cool, and then I wanted to give it a try. Adrian prepares for his first live performance. Image: adrian_jaams “So then I gave it a shot and I started going through acoustic at first and eventually went to electric.” Abraham added: “I used to play acoustic guitar and he used to sit down and listen. One day he told me he wanted to just hold the guitar to get the feel of it. “He took the guitar and he held a perfect cord. That’s the time I realised the guitar is the instrument for him. “His first guitar was a classic acoustic guitar which he played for about three months before it wasn’t enough for him and we had to upgrade to an electric. He is really progressing well. “I’ve been in choirs and I picked up the acoustic guitar when I was in college. It was just for fun and then I left it, but then when Adrian was born, I had this overwhelming feeling I should play something to him which would sound good. Music brings the out a real person. “But then he reached a point where he discovering grade eight. I can only teach him as much as basics of the guitar but the further grades, he picked it up himself.” With the help of a tutor, Adrian could now become the youngest person to pass the Grade 8 rock and pop guitar exam, setting a world record. He said: “I feel very excited and happy that I could be beating a world record, and I’m very happy that I got this far. If I beat it, I’m gonna be so overjoyed!” READ MORE: New drive to open car wash in town Adrian has been given a Marshall amplifier and Solar guitar by the manufacturers. Image: adrian_jaams While Adrian has to showcase a range of techniques for the exam, playing his favourite song is already a challenge for guitarists. With more than 200 beats per minute, it requires a tapping technique, using fingers from each hand, instead of picking or plucking. Adrian said: “My favourite song would be Eruption from Van Halen, and since I just really like the tapping pod and it just really gets me. It is the most-iconic tapping song in the world and it just sounds absolutely great.” The youngster’s ability has earned global attention, including endorsements from legendary music industry brands Marshall Amplifiers and Solar Guitars, which have supplied him with equipment to help his music journey. Following his exams, the natural outlet for Adrian’s talent would be playing in a band. Abraham said: “When people hear Adrian, a lot of them want him in a band, but by the time they see him, they’re like, he’s too little . . . his guitar is taller than him!” But Adrian is clear that music will be in his future. He said: “My dream would be to be the best guitarist in the world and be playing with famous bands and having fun with them too.” But playing the guitar has other benefits too. He added: “I usually just like it because it sounds good, it comes down my stress and it helps me play it and it helps me to just enjoy relax and play some good songs because usually most of the songs are heavy metal.” By sharing his journey on Instagram, Adrian and Abraham want to inspire others to do the same. Abraham said: “Like Adrian, you don’t have to wait to pick up a guitar. You can do it anytime, and you can’t, if Adrian can do it, so can you.” He joked: “I’ve got a daughter as well now she she’s only four years old, but she’s picked up the guitar because she thinks that’s the only way to get attention in the house!” Adrian and his dad, Abraham. articles.title: Rochdale Council plans major investments and heritage restoration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough.

With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

articles.title: Volunteers and council team tackle overgrown areas at Middleton’s Jubilee Park
articles.excerpt: The Friends of Jubilee Park and council staff have joined forces for the second phase of work to manage overgrown shrubs and care for the park’s rhododendrons.
articles.content_html:
Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

articles.title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
articles.excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
articles.content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

Sources: Facebook post attributed to Councillor Georgina Jacques, screenshot supplied to Rochdale Daily; council profile: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7226; Citizens Advice: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/law-and-courts/parking-tickets/when-to-appeal-a-parking-ticket/; POPLA: https://www.popla.co.uk/appeal-guide; CMA: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/parking-charges-cma-takes-action-to-drive-improvements-for-motorists

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

articles.title: Teenager jailed for fatal crash in Middleton after teaching himself to drive
articles.excerpt: An 18-year-old has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly.
articles.content_html:
A teenager has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly. Ruhul Islam, now 18, taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos and was behind the wheel of his brother's Nissan Micra when he struck Terence James, 78, on Shawbury Street on 29 September 2024.

During a hearing at Manchester Crown Court on 13 October 2026, it was revealed that Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries for a local business. Witnesses reported seeing him swerving through traffic, running red lights, and driving aggressively shortly before the crash.

Mr James was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter when he was hit, suffering severe injuries that led to his death the following day after life support was withdrawn.

Judge Kate Cornell described the vehicle as a 'dangerous weapon' in the hands of someone unqualified to drive. She stated that Mr James would likely still be alive had Islam adhered to traffic laws.

The court heard that Islam initially attempted to conceal his involvement in the crash, claiming his older brother was driving at the time.

Following the sentencing, it is expected that discussions around stricter enforcement of driving regulations may take place, although no specific measures have been announced yet.

articles.title: Rochdale Council announces new regeneration projects for Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has unveiled a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, including the restoration of Hopwood Hall and the acquisition of Warwick Mill.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, following a recent High Court judgement in favour of the council regarding Hopwood Hall. This decision brings clarity to the future of the historic building, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. The council is committed to funding essential repairs and considering options for its long-term future.

In addition to the Hopwood Hall project, the council has made significant strides in Middleton's regeneration ambitions. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to lead to the announcement of a new tenant before the end of the year. Furthermore, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be redeveloped for new housing, enhancing the local community.

Plans are also underway to transform the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue that will provide activities and training opportunities for young people.

The council has also confirmed that banking and post office services will return to Middleton town centre in the new year, a move that is anticipated to provide a boost to the local economy.

These initiatives are part of the council's broader commitment to invest in the borough, creating jobs and driving economic growth.

The council has also approved a £15 million support package over the next three years to assist residents facing financial difficulties, ensuring that help is available for those in need.

articles.excerpt: Duchy Homes’ Holtwood Green scheme comprises 56 homes on Manchester Old Road. The developer announced eight homes under the First Homes scheme, approximately 14.3% of the total, alongside a three- to five-bedroom market offer.
articles.content_html:
Duchy Homes’ Holtwood Green scheme comprises 56 homes on Manchester Old Road. The developer announced eight homes under the First Homes scheme, approximately 14.3% of the total, alongside a three- to five-bedroom market offer.

The live sales page reviewed advertises prices from £340,995 for a three-bedroom house, with larger properties priced higher. That opening market price should not be described as the price of the discounted First Homes. The eligible plots and their valuations need a separate schedule.

Discounted ownership gives some households a route to buy, but does not answer demand for social rent. Future purchasers also need mortgage eligibility, clear resale conditions and information on charges.

The council’s June 2026 update records construction. School places, healthcare capacity, drainage and transport obligations were not established from the material reviewed. Marketing claims about connectivity are useful context rather than an independent infrastructure assessment.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against Duchy was established. That does not certify the company’s entire legal history or replace scrutiny of warranties and aftercare.

The development contributes to the borough’s housing supply through actual completions. Its full 56 homes should not be treated as still outstanding if some are already occupied.

Eighty care-home beds cannot simply be added to twenty houses and advertised as one hundred ordinary family homes. Any contribution to the housing-delivery measure must use the applicable treatment of communal accommodation.

Access, staff and visitor travel, drainage and the relationship with nearby services are central infrastructure questions. No site-specific capacity assessment was verified here. The developer’s approval statement does not supply that evidence.

articles.title: Simister and Bowlee’s cross-border plan includes 200 homes in Rochdale, not 1,550
articles.excerpt: Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.
articles.content_html:
Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.

The development framework includes a new primary school in the Bury portion, a local centre, a spine road, off-site highway works, active-travel routes, green infrastructure and drainage measures. These are requirements and ambitions for a future neighbourhood, rather than proof that all funding and construction contracts are in place.

Bury’s website cites its own affordable policy rate and an approximate affordable total for the Bury homes. That percentage should not be automatically applied to the Rochdale share. The eventual cross-boundary applications need clear tenure schedules and allocation arrangements.

Residents campaigning against the development raise traffic and drainage concerns. Those are attributed concerns, not verified findings that infrastructure cannot accommodate the plan. The published assessments and conditions must show how risks are addressed.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

articles.title: High Court rules against filmmaker in Hopwood Hall restoration dispute
articles.excerpt: A recent High Court ruling has concluded a legal battle between American filmmaker Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council over the future of Hopwood Hall in Middleton.
articles.content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that American filmmaker Hopwood DePree does not have the right to purchase Hopwood Hall, a Grade-II* listed building in Middleton, following a protracted legal dispute with Rochdale Council. The decision was announced during a hearing at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, marking a significant setback for DePree, who has invested over £750,000 in efforts to restore the historic estate.

The saga began in 2017 when DePree signed an options agreement with the council to lead the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall. His vision included transforming the 1400s stately home into a wedding and hospitality venue, complete with a hotel retreat, gift shop, and guided tours.

DePree engaged the local community in his restoration efforts, which included extensive work on the hall's gardens and interior.

Before DePree's involvement, Hopwood Hall had fallen into disrepair, with its last known use being as part of De La Salle College, which closed in 1989.

The hall had previously served as a venue for various events, including an underground bar and nightclub during the 1960s and 70s, where notable acts such as Black Sabbath performed.

The ruling concludes a decade-long effort by DePree to revive the hall, which has been under the ownership of Rochdale Council since the college's closure. The future of Hopwood Hall now remains uncertain as the council considers its next steps regarding the estate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The Hopwood Hall saga | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The Hopwood Hall saga George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:44 AM Print The Grade-II listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton When an American filmmaker and Rochdale council signed an agreement over a shared ambition to restore Hopwood Hall, no one could have fathomed the furious saga that unfolded. What started as a harmonious relationship between Hopwood DePree and the local authority ended up with them being on opposite sides of a court room. Mr DePree claims ancestral connections to the Grade-II* listed building in Middleton. His dream was to bring the 1400s stately home back to life. He even roped in the local community to help him do it, apparently spending more than £750,000 on the project. On what he described as a ‘sad day’ in Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, his dream was crushed. The High Court ruled in favour of the council following a legal battle over whether Mr DePree had the right to buy the estate or not. The saga began in 2017 when Hopwood DePree signed an options agreement with town hall bosses to lead the redevelopment of the hall. Since then he has led a decade-long community effort to do exactly that. The Hollywood man’s vision saw the hall transformed into a wedding and hospitality venue, with a hotel ‘retreat’, gift shop and guided tours all part of the package. His team could regularly be seen working on the hall’s gardens and titivating the interior in the years since. Before Mr DePree came along, the hall had fallen into disrepair and irrelevance. Its last known use was as part of the De La Salle College, which shut down in 1989. During the 1960s and 70s it was said to be the setting for an underground bar and nightclub. It is believed that Ozzy Osbourne’s band Black Sabbath and other iconic performers played there. Since the closure of the college, the hall has been in the possession of Rochdale council. The American even created a Youtube series and wrote a book about his journey refurbishing what he affectionately called ‘Downton Shabby’. However, this journey came to an abrupt halt when the council ended the agreement in October 2024 and, without warning, barred Mr DePree and his group from the building. Part of the options agreement allowed the US actor and producer to purchase the historic asset from landowners Rochdale council for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Mr DePree attempted to exercise that option the day before the council ended the agreement, which was denied by town hall chiefs. Since then, a two-year-long war of words has raged between Mr DePree and Rochdale council. The American threatened legal action for months, but the council never budged. Mr DePree believed the local authority acted unlawfully by denying his ‘legally binding’ option to buy Hopwood Hall. At the time, the council said they ended the agreement because Mr DePree hadn’t made enough progress with the restoration effort. This expulsion from the estate came following a number of extensions to the agreement made by the council. The local authority even granted ‘change of use’ planning permission to Mr DePree for Hopwood Hall in 2022. Until the two sides decided to settle the matter in High Court, it was unclear just how important that planning permission was. Effectively, approved planning permission was the trigger to open up the option for Mr DePree to have the estate transferred to him. The High Court played host to Hopwood Hall Estate Ltd vs Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council this week. In the words of Mr DePree’s barrister, Ashley Bowes, the planning permission was ‘the star of the show’. The court heard details of the dispute over whether Mr DePree had authority to trigger the transfer of the property based on the approved plans. The council’s barrister Geraint Wheatley said the plans did not go far enough in demonstrating a serious commitment to reinstate and refurbish the 1400s building, as required by the options agreement. He described the ‘ruined’ hall as needing far more than some internal works to bring it back to a state of habitation. According to Mr Wheatley the conditions of the options agreement to trigger the purchase of the hall had four elements – authorisation to reinstate and refurbish the building; agreed standard of refurbishment between the parties (fit for habitation); English Heritage approval; and that the property would be reinstated and refurbished in whole, not in part. The defence barrister pointed out that getting permission for events and hospitality space for part of the ground floor doesn’t relate to the building ‘in whole’, as requested in the agreement clause. He also pointed out that the plans wouldn’t have seen the hall be fit for habitation or reinstated and refurbished. “Obtaining a mere ‘change of use’ permission doesn’t show a great deal of commitment,” Mr Wheatley told the court. “Plans of physical work show that commitment.” Mr Wheatley also tried to argue that English Heritage approval wasn’t given. But His Honour Judge Hodge KC believed the organisation’s support for the 2022 plans qualified as their approval. Buoyed by the judge agreeing with one point of the claimant, Dr Bowes said the 2022 application was internal work that would have created an events and hospitality space and enabled future work to be reinstated and refurbished. He said the claimant didn’t think anything more than a change of use application would be necessary to trigger the purchase as it wasn’t specified in the agreement. Dr Bowes said it was ‘wishful thinking’ on the council’s part that a community group would spend huge sums of money drawing up plans for physical works when they didn’t think it would be necessary. After delving into detailed planning legislation; the interpretation of wording in the agreement; and the cross-examinations of both Hopwood DePree and council boss for economy and place, Mark Robinson, the judge ruled in favour of the defendant – Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council. His Honour Judge Hodge KC described how the planning application did not cover the whole of the property or showcase the ability to reinstate and refurbish Hopwood Hall, as required in the options agreement. He added: “I am satisfied, for the reasons I have given, that the planning permission does not satisfy the requirements of the options agreement. I therefore refuse to grant the relief sought by the claimant.” A lengthy saga was ended by a two-day trial. Instead of getting Hopwood Hall for £1, Mr DePree was landed with a £114,000 bill to cover the council’s court costs. However, the American said the fight isn’t over and Hopwood Hall ‘must be saved’. He didn’t confirm whether his team would appeal the judgement, but they have until November 18 to do so. Speaking after the case, Mr DePree said: “Obviously I am incredibly disappointed. Not just me but the community of support around the world and the UK charitable groups as well. “I am already discussing with my legal team about the next steps. In the meantime I hope Rochdale council will be watching over Hopwood Hall because we will be keeping an eye on them. “We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved. In the two years we have been locked out the gardens have gone into wrack and ruin. I hope they will step up and save the hall. I still think the community group and I are the best people to take this forward. “I am getting messages from around the world with people offering money and support. It is a sad day but we will have to have a look at our options.” The town hall has committed to maintaining the building and have commissioned a feasibility study to look into possible future uses for the historic asset. A Rochdale council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6m has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “One thing we are clear on is, whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us?
